newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - World's biggest sale resumes in Russia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - World's biggest sale resumes in Russia.

text.p: The world's biggest sell-off is underway again in Russia as experienced privatisers previously accused of selling communist gems at knock-down prices auction companies worth billions of dollars.

With a new mandate from a healthy president, young reformers will sell stakes in leading Russian communications firms, the metals and oil industry, among others, at auctions intended to be open and fair.
Foreigners frozen out of many previous Russian privatisations are being given a few chances to bid and prices for major stakes look a lot healthier than in the past.
The highest profile bidders are a handful of companies led by well-connected businessmen-officials who built their reputations and fortunes in deals during the last wave of selling.

"The bottom line is Russia is not getting as much as the companies are worth," said a Western diplomat. "The auctions were set up in a way which leaves plenty of room for inside dealing and it is still that way."
Other analysts hotly disagree.

Peter Halloran, head of equities and research at CS First Boston in Moscow, said the appointment of First Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov in March was a watershed setting off a new wave of intelligent privatisation.

"Yeltsin was making a very strong move in one direction which we had not seen in the past," he said. "These guys understand it is important to have regulation, transparency and rules in the market. Everyone is on the same page."
STAKES STILL HIGH
The Russian government still owns huge stakes in major companies and intends to sell many soon.

Major stakes in oil groups Surgutneftegaz, YUKOS and Sibneft have been sold at auctions, while most Russian companies have been privatised and shares in many transferred to the public by convertible vouchers years ago.

The telephone industry will be transformed this week, when an auction for 25 percent of Svyazinvest, a company with controlling stakes in almost every regional operator, is sold at an auction open to foreigners and Russians.

"All the projects of the future depend on what happens in Svyazinvest," said Carlo Fucelli, Russian representative for Italy's Stet SpA communications, when asked about investment in Russia. "We are awaiting the role of Svyazinvest."
Stet won the Svyazinvest stake in an earlier auction at the end of 1995 but the deal fell apart on disagreement over terms.
U.S. professor Joseph Blasi, who directed a study into Russian privatisation, said that an average 21 percent stake in leading companies are still in government hands.

By any but previous Russian standards, that is a lot to privatise. Stakes in six major oil companies are now being sold and a 15 percent stake in Russia's largest producer, LUKoil, is due to be sold late this year or early next.
Stakes in the state oil company Rosneft and Rosgosstrakh, the country's biggest insurer, will eventually go on the block, though generally healthy minority interests are up for sale.

Privatisation minister Alfred Kokh, who has said fewer higher quality auctions will be held this year to maximise price, has said he will raise 11.4 trillion roubles ($2 billion) for the budget this year.
President Boris Yeltsin has recently ordered upwards of 13 trillion in back wages to be paid this year, partly through privatisation which may increase the pressure to sell.
A MANDATE TO PRIVATISE
Reformers are seen carrying out new privatisation in a way which will maximise state profits.
"Last year before the elections there was a rush to get it out the door," said a Western economist. "This year, there is a sense that doing it properly will bring money for the budget.
"The switch has been made from mass privatisation to case by case privatisation."
But despite healthy-looking prices, the terms and goals of the auctions beyond raising funds for the budget are not always clear.

"There is no evidence that the privatisation programme has set priorities," said the Western diplomat. Competing government and company claims on auction proceeds have not been resolved and no policy for improving management has been articulated.
Some say moving property into private hands is enough to get the country moving.

But an auction for a 38 percent stake in Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's leading producers of nickel and platinum, is attracting criticism and controversy. Up to the opening of bidding this week it was unclear if foreigners could take part.

"Without qualified competitive bids, one of Russia's industrial treasures will sold off at bargain basement prices," David Reuben, chairman of the British-based commodities firm Trans-World Group, said in a statement.

Trans-World, already active in the Russian metals industry, is considering a bid but said current auction conditions make the value of the stake unclear and termed the sale "the biggest mistake in the history of Russian industry".
FOREIGNERS - CASH COWS OR STRATEGIC PARTNERS
Foreigners have more money than Russians, which is the main reason they are allowed to compete in auctions, analysts say.
"They are more the cash cow than the strategic partner," the Western analyst said. "The Russians do not like giving up control and they are after money -- that is not unusual."
A few well-connected banks which won previous auctions for management of government owned stakes in the so-called loans for shares auctions of 1995 and 1996, are seen as lead contenders.
"It is generally a game only for powerful structures," said United City Bank banking analyst Andrei Yashchenko.

The best chance for small companies and foreigners will be to work with Russian groups, meeting the government's need for cash with its preference for locals, he said. "There needs to be some real money which Russian banks do not have a lot of right now." ($=5,786 roubles)
